models.collectorNote: Early small-mouth TR3s and disc-brake cars are prized; overdrive gearboxes transform them and add value in kind.

generations.name: TR2 / TR3 / TR3A
generations.note: The TR2's 90 hp grew to 100 in the TR3A, which also brought the full-width grille and front disc brakes, standard from 1956, a production-car first generation when it mattered.

models.intro: The post-war British sports car distilled: a twin-carburettor twin-seater with cut-down doors, a 100 mph top speed and a price Detroit couldn't touch. The TR line started here, and so did a generation of American sports-car racing.
models.name: TR2 / TR3
models.photoCredit: Photo: Daniel Milner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Milner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: A genuine TR5 PI is the blue-chip small TR. Verify the injection system is present and working, many were converted to carburettors, and the market prices accordingly.

generations.name: TR4 / TR4A
generations.note: The TR4A added independent rear suspension. The four-cylinder TRs are the last of the tractor-engine line, torquey, simple, indestructible.

generations.name: TR5 PI / TR250
generations.note: Lucas fuel injection gave the home-market TR5 150 hp and a genuine 120 mph; the federal TR250 made do with twin carburettors and 104 hp. Just 2,947 TR5s were built.

models.intro: Michelotti civilised the TR: wind-up windows, a proper boot, and an optional Surrey top, then the TR5 added fuel injection and six cylinders' worth of pace. America got carburettors and the TR250 name instead, which is why the injected cars are the legend.
models.name: TR4 / TR5 / TR250
models.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 1962 Triumph TR4 (54803)
photos.credit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Chassis outriggers and trailing-arm mounts rust structurally, the frame inspection matters more than the paint. Injected cars lead, US cars follow closely on condition.

generations.name: TR6
generations.note: Home-market injected cars made 150 hp, then 125 from 1973; US carburettor cars were rated 104 hp. The gap is the whole story of seventies emissions law in one model.

models.intro: Karmann sharpened the TR5's suit and Triumph kept the recipe: a big six, a separate chassis, and 150,000 buyers, nearly all of them American. The last of the traditional hairy-chested TRs before the wedge arrived.
models.name: TR6
models.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 1971 Triumph TR6 (15638)
photos.credit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: TR8s are genuinely scarce and priced like it; TR7s remain the cheapest seat in the TR club. Check wedge sills and turrets before the cosmetics.

generations.name: TR7
generations.note: UK cars made 105 hp, US cars less under emissions tuning. Convertibles arrived in 1979 and are the better drive and the easier sell.

generations.name: TR8
generations.note: The V8 the wedge always needed, built mostly for America and mostly as a convertible. Official production was under 3,000 cars.

models.intro: 'The shape of things to come': Harris Mann's wedge replaced a decade of tradition with pop-up lamps and a fixed head, and the launch quality troubles wrote the headlines. The TR8's Rover V8 fixed the pace problem just as production ended, which is why it is the one everyone wants now.
models.name: TR7 / TR8
models.photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 1975 Triumph TR7, front 3/4
photos.credit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Condition rules a market this deep; a sorted 1500 is the usable classic, an early Mk III the prettiest. Sills and bonnet fit tell you the car's real history.

generations.name: Spitfire 4 / Mk II / Mk III
generations.note: The Herald's 1147 cc engine made 63 hp in twin-carburettor tune; the Mk III's 1296 cc raised it to 75 and added the raised front bumper the Americans required.

generations.name: Spitfire Mk IV / 1500
generations.note: The Mk IV cleaned up the tail and tamed the rear suspension; the 1500's longer-stroke engine traded revs for torque, with US cars rated lower under emissions rules.

models.intro: Michelotti's small sports car on Herald bones: a flip-forward bonnet, swing axles with opinions, and 315,000 buyers over eighteen years. The Spitfire was the sports car students could afford and the one half the paddock started in.
models.name: Spitfire

models.collectorNote: Buy the engine history, not the paint: a Stag with a paper trail of timing-chain and head work is worth more than a shiny one without.

generations.name: Stag
generations.note: About 26,000 were built. The V8's timing chains and cooling are the known work; cars with documented engine rebuilds and modern cooling upgrades are the market's preference, not its compromise.

models.intro: Triumph's grand idea: a four-seat convertible with a home-grown 3.0 V8, a T-bar roof and Michelotti styling aimed squarely at Mercedes' SL. The engine's cooling troubles wrote its reputation; the survivors, mostly cured by forty years of club knowledge, are the grand tourers the car always meant to be.
models.name: Stag
models.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Sprints are the collectible; verify the Sprint engine is present, the sixteen-valve head is the value, and a standard engine under the bonnet is a known swap.

generations.name: Dolomite / Dolomite Sprint
generations.note: The Sprint's single-cam sixteen-valve head made 127 hp in 1973, when that was BMW 2002 tii territory. About 23,000 Sprints were built.

models.intro: The Sprint is the headline: a 2.0-litre sixteen-valve head, the first mass-produced multi-valve engine, on a Michelotti sedan that embarrassed bigger cars in touring-car racing. The ordinary Dolomites were worthy family cars; the Sprint was a factory hot rod in a cardigan.
